text:
A person is taking part in a study. They read moral dilemmas one at a time. For each one
they answer Yes or No to the question at the end. They are then told what happened as a
result, and they rate how good or bad the consequences were, from -100 (very bad) to 100
(very good).

Here are records from other people in the same study.

Person A:
Dilemma:
You are a member of the Canadian Senate and have to vote on a new law. Canada’s health care expenses are increasing steadily, mainly because the ratio of old people increases. Recent studies indicate that the legalization of medically assisted suicide would strongly decrease medical expenses. The state considers legalizing medically assisted suicide for the patients who are terminally ill and whose life expectancy is 6 months or less. If they wish, these patients could then choose to be killed by a doctor with an overdose of tranquillizers. Experts estimate that the new law would save 139 million dollars. This money could be used for other medical treatments. If you allow medically assisted suicide, many more people will get better medical treatment improving their quality of life and life expectancy. However, you would legalize a form of killing. If you do not allow medically assisted suicide, the healthcare system will have to keep on saving money in every possible way. Do you change the law and make medically assisted suicide legal?
Answer: Yes
What happened: You change the law and make medically assisted suicide legal. However, terminally ill patients rarely take up this option as they are afraid of the additional suffering that the medically assisted suicide may induce. As a result, the healthcare system does not get additional funding, and not enough money is available for other patients. In the end, you legalized a form of killing, and your actions do not save any funds and many patients die due to low healthcare funding.
Rating: -100

Dilemma:
You are a European veterinarian conducting animal experiments on highly contagious germs. On a daily basis, you cause suffering to animals by infecting them with deadly diseases. You are aware that this work provides important insights that, in the long run, can save many other animals. Furthermore, you are a specialist and because of your expertise you can achieve more than other veterinarians. However, you have become a vet in order to heal animals and you are considering quitting your job. If you quit your job, fewer animals will die in the lab, but there will also be fewer findings about animal diseases. As a result, the development of medicines for healing sick animals will be delayed, leading to many preventable deaths. If you continue your job of infecting animals with diseases for medical research, you will keep causing animal suffering, but your research will probably save the lives of even more animals in the future. Do you quit your job?
Answer: Yes
What happened: You quit your job as a veterinarian. As a result, your lab closes down and this research is discontinued, and any animals you had kept for testing were euthanized. A few years later, you come across a report which shows that most research in this area is basically worthless and many basic results could not be reproduced. You realise that while you had inflicted some suffering on animals, many lives were spared because your research was discontinued. In the end, your decision saves the lives of animals who would have potentially suffered and died - but you harmed some animals in the process.
Rating: 100

Dilemma:
It is 1841, and you are the captain of a ship. After colliding with an iceberg, the ship sank. You, some other crew members, and passengers were able to save yourselves onto two lifeboats. The next day, it starts to rain. You navigate while the others scoop out the water and oar. Someone from the other lifeboat calls to you, and you say that they are overcrowded with 41 people. The large waves could make their lifeboat sink at any time and the passengers ask you what to do as you are the highest ranking officer. You think that approximately ten adults would have to leave the boat to substantially increase the chance that the other passengers will survive. However, your lifeboat is already at full capacity and you cannot accept any more passengers. The 10 passengers would have to go overboard, and you know that the water is so cold that they would freeze to death. If you tell them not to throw anybody overboard, the boat will most likely sink at some point within the next few days and all 41 people will die. If you instead tell them to throw 10 people overboard, the rest of the passengers will be able to keep rowing towards land and will have a good chance of being rescued. Do you ask them to throw 10 people overboard?
Answer: Yes

Person B:
Dilemma:
You are a European veterinarian conducting animal experiments on highly contagious germs. On a daily basis, you cause suffering to animals by infecting them with deadly diseases. You are aware that this work provides important insights that, in the long run, can save many other animals. Furthermore, you are a specialist and because of your expertise you can achieve more than other veterinarians. However, you have become a vet in order to heal animals and you are considering quitting your job. If you quit your job, fewer animals will die in the lab, but there will also be fewer findings about animal diseases. As a result, the development of medicines for healing sick animals will be delayed, leading to many preventable deaths. If you continue your job of infecting animals with diseases for medical research, you will keep causing animal suffering, but your research will probably save the lives of even more animals in the future. Do you quit your job?
Answer: No
What happened: You continue working as a veterinarian. A few years later, you come across a report which shows that most research in this area is basically worthless and its results cannot be reproduced. You realise that you had inflicted pointless suffering on those animals with little to no benefit. In the end, your actions caused many more animals to suffer and die.
Rating: -100

Dilemma:
You are the German head of state and 10 of your citizens are taken hostage in the Sahara Desert by a group of terrorists. You have to decide whether to pay a ransom of several million euros. Other measures to free the hostages have been tried but did not succeed; by now, it has been going on for half a year and one woman has died. Similar situations in the past have shown that terrorists use the money to buy weapons and kill even more people. Furthermore, future tourists will more likely be kidnapped if you pay. If you pay the ransom, you can save the hostages. If you do not pay, the 10 hostages will be killed, but you will prevent future terrorism being financed, which will probably save more than 10 lives. Do you pay the ransom?
Answer: No

Here is the record of the person you are asked about.

Dilemma:
You are the German head of state in 1977 and a far-left terrorist group kidnapped the President of the Federation of the German Employers’ Association. In exchange for his life, the terrorist group demands the release of 11 imprisoned members. A few years ago, the terrorist group had successfully obtained the release of 5 members by another kidnapping. 4 of the released members have since then committed further terrorist attacks that killed several innocent people. If you consent to the terrorist group’s demands, 11 former terrorists will be released and will likely commit further terrorist attacks killing several people. If you refuse, the hostage will be killed. Do you release the former terrorists?
Answer: No
What happened: You do not release the 11 former terrorists. The terrorist group kills the hostage and orchestrates an attack on his family members, and one person is severely injured. In the end, your decision does not save anyone: the hostage dies, and the terrorist attack leads to the injury of an innocent person.
Rating: 1

Dilemma:
You are a physician in a hospital in a town in a rural area. Your hospital needs to perform at least 50 lung surgeries per year in order to have them refunded by health insurance. Until this December, the hospital has only conducted 48 surgeries; thus, maybe none of the surgeries will be covered by insurance. The clinic has already been in debt the previous year and will have to file for bankruptcy if there will be another debt when the knee surgeries are not refunded. Without this hospital, the region will not have access to fast intensive emergency care. Sooner or later, having no fast access to intensive emergency care will lead to avoidable deaths in the region. The only way of sustaining the clinic would be by performing two lung surgeries that are medically not indicated. If you perform two unnecessary surgeries, you can save the hospital from bankruptcy and the region will continue to have fast emergency care, but you will perform surgery on two patients for whom other treatments would be more appropriate. If you do not perform the surgeries, the clinic will be closed leading to deaths sooner or later. Do you perform the two surgeries that are not medically indicated?
Answer: No
What happened: You do not perform the two lung surgeries. When the hospital is about to be shut down, the Ministry of Health provides additional funds to keep the hospital running. However, this funding is less than what you would have otherwise received from the insurance, resulting in reduced quality of care. In the end, your actions sustain fast emergency healthcare for the region - but the quality of care is reduced.
Rating: 23

Dilemma:
It is 1841, and you are the captain of a ship. After colliding with an iceberg, the ship sank. You, some other crew members, and passengers were able to save yourselves onto two lifeboats. The next day, it starts to rain. You navigate while the others scoop out the water and oar. Someone from the other lifeboat calls to you, and you say that they are overcrowded with 41 people. The large waves could make their lifeboat sink at any time and the passengers ask you what to do as you are the highest ranking officer. You think that approximately ten adults would have to leave the boat to substantially increase the chance that the other passengers will survive. However, your lifeboat is already at full capacity and you cannot accept any more passengers. The 10 passengers would have to go overboard, and you know that the water is so cold that they would freeze to death. If you tell them not to throw anybody overboard, the boat will most likely sink at some point within the next few days and all 41 people will die. If you instead tell them to throw 10 people overboard, the rest of the passengers will be able to keep rowing towards land and will have a good chance of being rescued. Do you ask them to throw 10 people overboard?
Answer: Yes
What happened: You tell the passengers to throw 10 people overboard. They do as you instruct and you watch as 10 randomly selected people are tossed into the water, where they will freeze and die. The rest of the passengers continue to row but it is obvious that they are distressed by what they did. A few days pass and the passengers still have low morale. When a strong wind rocks the boat, they are afraid that more people will be thrown overboard and start fighting amongst themselves, causing the boat to topple over. In the end, your decision does not save anyone: you watch as the lifeboat sinks and all the passengers die.
Rating: -41

Dilemma:
You are the German head of state and 10 of your citizens are taken hostage in the Sahara Desert by a group of terrorists. You have to decide whether to pay a ransom of several million euros. Other measures to free the hostages have been tried but did not succeed; by now, it has been going on for half a year and one woman has died. Similar situations in the past have shown that terrorists use the money to buy weapons and kill even more people. Furthermore, future tourists will more likely be kidnapped if you pay. If you pay the ransom, you can save the hostages. If you do not pay, the 10 hostages will be killed, but you will prevent future terrorism being financed, which will probably save more than 10 lives. Do you pay the ransom?
Answer: No
What happened: You do not pay the ransom to the terrorists. The terrorists kill the hostages. The leader of a more prominent terrorist group hears of this and decides to join forces with them, ensuring that they have funds for future attacks. In the end, your actions lead to the deaths of all the hostages, and the terrorists now have resources for future attacks.
Rating: -20

Current dilemma:
After a long-term imprisonment, a convicted child kidnapper and murderer wants to organise a foundation for young victims of crime. You are the president of the agency who decides about the foundation. The founder would donate of 25,000 euros to the foundation. However, the foundation would be named after the offender, and it is unclear whether he is acting out of remorse or simply to clear his name. The family of his victim opposes such a foundation and considers it immoral, derogatory, and an exploitation of the victim. If you oppose the foundation, the money will be lost. If you approve the foundation, crime victims will benefit from the 25,000 euros and additional fund raising. Do you approve the foundation?

Which answer does this person give to the current dilemma?
Answer with one word: Yes or No.
